title: Some Strategies for Learning to Teach Challenging Classes Well
author: Debbie Thompson
summary: Debbie Thompson, a maths and computer science teacher with more than 30 years in English schools, reflects on what kept her going through difficult classes and heavy workloads. She recalls starting her career by laying down rules before building rapport, and credits an older colleague with teaching her to greet students, learn names, and use 'I' statements. Facing an especially challenging class without senior support, she kept a reflective diary that helped her plan and slowly regain control. She describes predictable routines such as a silent starter task, and learning to defuse power struggles with a calm 'We'll talk about this later.' Thompson is frank that many school behaviour procedures, like break-time detentions and names on the board, exhausted teachers without changing behaviour, and she recounts persuading a new headteacher to cut meaningless weekly data analysis. She closes with the value of small wins, shared planning, and staffroom connection as anchors of motivation.
points: Building rapport before enforcing rules, through greetings, names, and interest in students' lives, turned around her first difficult class.
A weekly reflective diary helped her plan a way forward when sanctions and senior support failed.
Some behaviour policies, like keeping students back at break, exhausted teachers without changing repeat misbehaviour.
She persuaded a headteacher to outsource weekly test analysis, arguing progress cannot be measured in weekly portions.
A shared lesson planning bank cut preparation time by about half and built collegial connection.
quotes: The problem was that I didn’t realise that building rapport early on was also important.
When sanctions didn’t work, and there was no support available from senior staff, I found that it was good to keep a diary that gave me space to reflect on what was happening.
I learned that I knew more about classroom management than I thought I did, and I learned that careful reflection and good planning based on that can work well.

By then I had noticed that those 10-minute chats didn’t change the behaviour of most of the students who were repeatedly difficult in a lesson. I needed to take a different approach to working with these students.
I told her that more time spent in the classroom teaching would help results improve and that analysing weekly results from tests that teachers were compelled to give students was meaningless.

When I was a newly qualified teacher, I had a win jar on my desk, and every time something good happened, like a student breakthrough, a compliment, or a bit of shared laughter in my lesson, I wrote it down on a piece of paper and dropped it in.
But all teachers need space to breathe and to be able to choose to connect with other teachers so that they can develop the craft of teaching in a supportive environment.
